text: Sargent's Portrait of Madame X was meant to cement his place as a Paris society painter, and it caused a scandal instead. He was born in Florence to American parents and trained there and in Paris. After the scandal he moved to England, where his portrait career took off again. He made roughly 900 oil paintings and more than 2,000 watercolors, along with countless sketches. Art historians mostly ignored society painters like him until the late 20th century. An exhibition of his male nudes in the 1980s started a fresh look at his life.

At 11, Paul Klee was good enough on the violin to be invited to play with the Bern Music Association. His father taught music and his mother sang. Everyone expected him to follow them. He chose the visual arts as a teenager, partly out of rebellion. From 1897 he kept a diary, and scholars still use it to follow his thinking. Later he taught at the Bauhaus alongside Wassily Kandinsky, and his lectures on form and colour were published in English as the Paul Klee Notebooks.

Jan van Eyck signed ten of his paintings with the motto ALS ICH KAN, a pun on his name that he usually wrote in Greek letters. He was already a master with assistants when he went to work for John III at The Hague around 1422. Later he became court painter to Philip the Good and moved to Bruges in 1429. Philip sent him on diplomatic trips, including one to Lisbon to discuss a marriage. About 20 surviving paintings are confidently attributed to him. Vasari called him the inventor of oil painting, but that claim is now seen as too simple.

Robert Jenkins Onderdonk went to Texas in 1878 hoping to paint portraits of rich locals and save enough to travel to Europe. He had studied in New York under William Merritt Chase and James Carroll Beckwith. He ended up staying 38 years. In that time he painted, taught art in San Antonio and Dallas, and helped start the first art clubs in the state. One was the Brass Mug Club, a group of San Antonio artists who went out sketching together. People came to call him the Dean of Texas's Artists.

Tsuchiya Koitsu moved to Tokyo from Hamamatsu when he was 15. He first tried to become a temple apprentice, then took a place at an engraving studio. There he met Kobayashi Kiyochika and studied under him for 19 years, living in his house. His early prints showed scenes from the First Sino-Japanese War. He was already 60 when he started working for the publisher Shozaburo Watanabe, who also printed Kawase Hasui and Yoshida Hiroshi. His later landscapes use light to hit harder emotionally.

Armand Guillaumin worked in his uncle's lingerie shop and took drawing lessons in the evenings. At the Académie Suisse he met Paul Cézanne and Camille Pissarro. The three stayed friends for life. For a while he and Cézanne had studios next door to each other on the Île Saint-Louis, and Cézanne's only etchings, made in 1873, include one of Guillaumin. Guillaumin took part in six of the eight Impressionist exhibitions. The critic Félix Fénéon called him a furious colourist.

Giulio Clovio left his village of Grižane in Croatia for Italy at 18. There he joined the household of Cardinal Marino Grimani and was trained as a painter. He also studied under Giulio Romano, and he engraved medals and seals for Grimani's uncle. By 1524 he was in Buda at the Hungarian court of King Louis II, painting a Judgment of Paris and a Lucretia. After Louis died at the Battle of Mohács, Clovio went back to Rome. He is considered the greatest illuminator of the Italian High Renaissance.

Alexandre Cabanel was a carpenter's son who began at the Montpellier School of Fine Arts and moved to Paris on a scholarship in 1839. He failed twice to win the Prix de Rome, then took it at 22. Napoleon III liked him best of all painters, and with Gérôme and Meissonier he counted among the three most successful artists of the Second Empire. His private life was harder. His first wife and two of their children died in 1867, and his second wife died four years after he married her. The Birth of Venus brought him more recognition.

Dong Qichang passed the prefectural entrance exam at 12. He took the imperial exam for the first time at 17 and placed second to a cousin because his calligraphy was clumsy. That led him to train until he became a noted calligrapher. He passed the highest level at 35 and rose to a post at the Ministry of Rites. It wasn't a smooth career. In 1605 the candidates protested against him while he was giving the exam. An angry mob later burned his house down after he beat women who had come to him with grievances.

Jean Lemaire painted the architecture and Nicolas Poussin the figures, and that partnership earned him the nickname Lemaire-Poussin. He was born in Dammartin-en-Goële and studied under Claude Vignon before moving to Rome. Around 1636 he proposed a scholarly classical landscape for the Buen Retiro palace of Philip IV of Spain. Back in Paris, he became Poussin's main assistant on the Grande Galerie of the Louvre. Later he was made guardian of the king's paintings at the Louvre and the Tuileries. He died in Gaillon.

LaVerne Nelson Black painted Native Americans. He was born in Wisconsin, lived in Taos, New Mexico in the 1920s, and moved to Phoenix, Arizona in the next decade. In Phoenix he did two murals for the United States Post Office. His paintings are in the Denver Art Museum, the Fred Jones Jr. Museum of Art, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum. The Smithsonian holds Ceremonial at Black Lake and Jicarilla Apache Fiesta.

Jeremiah Meyer was brought from Tübingen to England in 1750 by his father, a painter. He is said to have worked in George Michael Moser's London workshop, decorating lockets and jewellery boxes with enamel. Moser's place was a meeting spot for German painters. That helped his English along. Later he paid £400 to study enamel painting with Christian Friedrich Zincke. He became Painter in Miniatures to Queen Charlotte and Painter in Enamels to George III. He was also a founder member of the Royal Academy.

Charles Verlat was the son of a soap and oil manufacturer in Antwerp. His mother arranged his first drawing lessons with a Dutch sculptor. He left school at 14 to study in Nicaise de Keyser's private studio. Verlat became best known for animals and portraits, but he also painted Orientalist scenes and religious subjects. In 1886 he was director of the Antwerp Academy, where he taught drawing, when Vincent van Gogh spent a short time there. The two men argued about Van Gogh's unconventional way of drawing.

Verner Thomé was one of eight children born to a forestry officer in Alajärvi, Finland. His first job was at a lithographic company that commissioned posters from Finnish artists. He studied drawing under Helene Schjerfbeck but left because of poor health. For several summers he stayed with Magnus Enckell on the island of Hogland. Then he travelled. In 1904 he visited Paris, Spain and Morocco, and when he got home he painted with a darker palette. He was influenced by Vitalism, a German-Scandinavian movement built on Nietzsche's philosophy.

Bernardo Bellotto was Canaletto's nephew and trained in his workshop. He sometimes signed his paintings Bernardo Canaletto, and in Germany and Poland he simply called himself Canaletto. That caused confusion. His colours are more somber than his uncle's, and his clouds and shadows are closer to Dutch painting. King Augustus III invited him to Dresden, where he spent about a decade. His views of the city now preserve a memory of buildings destroyed by bombing in World War II. He ended up as court painter in Warsaw for some 16 years, until his death.

Hieronymus Bosch left no letters or diaries, so nobody knows what he thought about his own art. What survives are brief mentions in the town records of 's-Hertogenbosch and in the account books of a local religious brotherhood. He was born in his grandfather's house. His grandfather was a painter, and so were four of the grandfather's five sons. Bosch signed some paintings Jheronimus Bosch. Only about 25 paintings and eight drawings are confidently identified as his. The best known are three triptych altarpieces, particularly The Garden of Earthly Delights.

William Victor Higgins was born in Shelbyville, Indiana. At 15 he moved to Chicago to study at the Art Institute. In Paris he was a pupil of Robert Henri. He moved to Taos, New Mexico in 1913, joined the Taos Society of Artists a few years later, and often painted portraits of Native American women there. During the Depression he was commissioned to paint a mural in the Taos County Courthouse, titled Moises, El Legislador. His first wife was Sara Parsons, and he was later briefly married to Marion Koogler McNay.

Giorgione died in his thirties, and almost everything known about his life comes from Giorgio Vasari. He came from the small town of Castelfranco Veneto. His name is a nickname that can be translated as Big George. Carlo Ridolfi says he served his apprenticeship in Venice under Giovanni Bellini. Only about six surviving paintings are firmly attributed to him. Together with the younger Titian he founded the Venetian school of painting, which is known for its use of colour and mood.

Carl Gottlieb Peschel paid for a study trip to Rome with part of his father's military pension. When he came home he made a living giving drawing lessons and painting snuff cans. Then the Saxon Art Association bought his painting Eliezer and Rebecca at the Well, and he could work full time. He took over the frescoes at the Härtel House in Leipzig after Bonaventura Genelli got into several quarrels and walked off the job. Later he painted scenes from Goethe's works at a manor called Belvedere. He became a professor at the Dresden Academy in 1846.

Henry Fuseli was the second of 18 children in a Zürich family. His father, a painter, meant him for the church, and Fuseli took orders. Then he helped his friend Johann Kaspar Lavater expose an unjust magistrate, and the magistrate's powerful family wanted revenge. Fuseli had to leave the country. He ended up in Britain, where he painted supernatural scenes such as The Nightmare. He made pictures for Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery and for his own Milton Gallery. He later became Professor of Painting and Keeper at the Royal Academy.

Almost everything about Giotto's life is disputed. Two things are certain. He painted the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, which was finished around 1305, and in 1334 the city of Florence chose him to design the new bell tower of its cathedral. The banker Giovanni Villani wrote that Giotto drew all his figures according to nature. Vasari went further and said Giotto broke with the Byzantine style and started drawing accurately from life.

Arent Arentsz. was born and died in Amsterdam and was buried in the Oude Kerk. He was also known as Cabel. According to the RKD he signed his works with the monogram AA. He painted summer and winter landscapes, mostly hunting and fishing scenes. Hendrick Avercamp influenced him, but their pictures are easy to tell apart. Some of his work can be seen at the National Gallery in London and at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

Hugo Charlemont came from a family of artists. His father Matthias Adolf Charlemont painted miniatures, his brothers Eduard and Theodor were painters, and his daughter Lilly became an artist too. He was born in Jemnice in Moravia and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1873 under Eduard von Lichtenfels. He painted landscapes, still lifes, animals, portraits and scenes of everyday life. One of his works is Interieur with a forge. He died in Vienna.

Isaac Levitan was born in a shtetl in what is now Lithuania, into a poor but educated Jewish family. The family moved to Moscow when he was a boy, and in 1873 he entered the city's school of painting. His older brother Avel was already a student there. His teachers included Alexei Savrasov, Vasily Perov and Vasily Polenov. In 1875 his mother died, and his father followed two years later. The family slid into abject poverty. Levitan went on to advance the genre of the mood landscape.

Sano di Pietro ran a busy workshop in Siena for about half a century. He didn't only paint altarpieces. The shop also produced frescoes, miniatures and book bindings. Sano was part of the civic fabric of the city too, and he twice led the San Donato district. In 1475 he was called in to settle a dispute between the painters Neroccio di Bartolommeo and Francesco di Giorgio Martini. His contemporaries included Giovanni di Paolo and Sassetta.

Elisabetta Sirani was one of the first women artists in early modern Bologna. Her father Giovanni Andrea was an art merchant and painter, and a favorite assistant of Guido Reni. At first he wasn't inclined to take his daughter as a pupil, but she picked up his technique anyway and trained in his studio. She produced public altarpieces as well as privately commissioned pictures. She died in unexplained circumstances at 27.

Very little is known about Xia Gui. No record survives of his birth and death dates, his background or his education. He was most probably born in Hangzhou, then the capital of Southern Song. Together with Ma Yuan he founded the Ma-Xia school. Only a few of his works survive, yet he is generally considered one of China's greatest artists. The Japanese master Sesshū was one of the artists who carried on his tradition into the early 17th century.

Miyagawa Chōshun founded the Miyagawa school. He and his pupils are among the few ukiyo-e artists who never made woodblock prints. He was born in Owari Province but spent much of his later life in Edo, where he died. He trained under artists of the Tosa and Kanō schools and under Hishikawa Moronobu. His works are almost all of courtesans, fuller and more voluptuous than most. Richard Lane thinks his coloring is among the best in ukiyo-e.

Francesco Montemezzano was born near Verona and seems to have followed Paolo Veronese, if he wasn't his pupil. He worked in Venice and on the mainland, painting mostly sacred subjects. He finished some of the panels for the church of San Nicolò dei Mendicoli. The biographer Ridolfi says he gave himself too much to the pleasures of love and to expensive objects, and that this led to an early death by poisoning. In 2015 the BBC show Fake or Fortune? investigated a Lamentation of Christ in an English church and verified it as his.

Charles-Antoine Coypel grew up in a family of successful history painters. His grandfather Noël had directed the French Academy in Rome, and his father Antoine received many commissions from the royal family. From his father he inherited the title of Keeper of the paintings and drawings of the king. It combined the roles of director and curator of the royal art collection. He became court painter and director of the Académie Royale. He also worked as an art critic and a playwright.

Felix Meyer was a Swiss landscape painter and engraver from Winterthur. He went to Nuremberg to study painting and met Georg Philipp Rugendas there. Back home he painted the mountains and glaciers around Winterthur. He also took part in local politics, first as First Sergeant and then, in 1697, as a member of the Grand Council. For a few years he lived in Bern. Later he returned to Winterthur and worked as a steward at Wyden Castle.

Imao Keinen got a broad education in Japanese painting, printmaking and calligraphy from the age of 12. In 1880 he became a professor at the Kyoto School of Painting. He joined the Art Committee of the imperial court after publishing an album of bird-and-flower woodblock prints, and he was appointed an Imperial Household Artist. His works are in museum collections around the world.

Fernand Khnopff painted his sister Marguerite again and again. She appears in portrait after portrait across his career. He was one of the founding members of the group Les XX in 1883, and he befriended Edward Burne-Jones and other British artists. After he showed 21 works at the first Vienna Secession exhibition, his Caress of the Sphinx influenced Gustav Klimt. He designed theater sets and opera costumes too, working with the director Max Reinhardt.

Juan Gris was born José Victoriano González-Pérez in Madrid. He first studied engineering and drew for local periodicals. Then he studied painting for a year with José Moreno Carbonero, and in 1905 he took the name Juan Gris. Most of his career was spent in France. In Paris he lived at the Bateau-Lavoir with his wife Lucie and their only child, in the years before the First World War. His works are among the most distinctive of Cubism.

Henry Luyten was born in Roermond in the Netherlands and became a Belgian painter. He studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp. Then came Paris. He took classes at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts there but came back to Antwerp after ten months, and in 1884 he joined an art circle called Als ik kan. His main friends in the circle were Henri van de Velde, Jan-Willem Rosier and Leon Brunin. He painted genre scenes, marines, landscapes, portraits and animals.

Umberto Boccioni was born in Reggio Calabria, the son of a minor government employee whose job meant constant moves. He grew up in Forlì, Genoa and Padua with his older sister Amelia. At 15 he moved with his father to Catania in Sicily, where he finished school. He became one of the principal figures of Futurism, as both painter and sculptor. He died in 1916. His life was short, but in 1988 the Metropolitan Museum of Art still organized a retrospective of 100 pieces.

Gerrit Dou was the son of a stained-glass maker in Leiden, and he trained in a stained-glass workshop himself. In February 1628, at fourteen, his father sent him to study painting with Rembrandt, who lived nearby and was about 21. Dou stayed with him for about three years. From Rembrandt he learned colouring and the subtler effects of chiaroscuro. He went on to specialise in small, highly polished pictures, trompe-l'œil niche paintings and candlelit night scenes.

Bernhard Keil was born in Helsingør in Denmark and first studied with the painter Morten Steenwinkel. According to the RKD he then went to Amsterdam and became a pupil of Rembrandt. After that he spent a few years with Hendrick Uylenburgh and ran a workshop of his own. In 1656 he travelled to Rome and stayed there for the rest of his life. He also worked in Bergamo and Venice. Jan Lievens influenced him, and he in turn influenced Pietro Bellotti, Antonio Cifrondi and Giacomo Francesco Cipper.

Nainsukh was the younger son of the painter Pandit Seu, and his older brother Manaku was a painter too. Around 1740 he left the family workshop in Guler and moved to Jasrota. There he painted most of his works for the local Rajput ruler Mian Zorowar Singh and then for the ruler's son Balwant Singh. This is the best known and best documented phase of his career. He brought Mughal elements into Pahari painting, which had mainly been concerned with Hindu religious subjects. He has been called one of the most original and brilliant of Indian painters.

Jean-Marc Nattier was the second son of a portrait painter and a miniaturist. His uncle was the history painter Jean Jouvenet. As a young man he copied pictures in the Luxembourg Palace, making drawings of Rubens's Marie de' Medici cycle. When engravings of those drawings were published in 1710, he became famous. He turned down the chance to go on to the French Academy in Rome, even though he had taken first prize at the Paris Academy at fifteen. He is noted for portraits of the ladies of Louis XV's court dressed as mythological figures.

Józef Brandt went to Paris in 1858 to study engineering. Juliusz Kossak persuaded him to give it up for painting. Brandt went on to study in Munich under Franz Adam and Karl Piloty, and then he opened his own studio. He was born in Szczebrzeszyn and painted battles from Polish history, often with horses. Most of his pictures show military life in the 17th century, though he also made some studies of Polish peasant life.

Maruyama Ōkyo was born into a farming family and moved to Kyoto as a teenager. He apprenticed at a toy shop, where he painted the faces onto dolls. The shop also sold European stereoscopes, and looking into one was his first sight of Western perspective. He later studied Chinese, Japanese and Western artworks. Out of that came a personal style that mixed Western naturalism with Eastern decorative design, and he founded the Maruyama school. Many fellow artists said his work was too slavishly devoted to natural representation, but it proved a success with laypeople.

Jean-Étienne Liotard was born in Geneva to French Huguenots in exile. He worked in Rome, Istanbul, Paris, Vienna, London and Amsterdam, among other cities. After visiting Turkey he wore a full beard, which was an eccentricity in 18th century Europe. He made detailed, naturalistic portraits in pastel, and scenes of life in Turkey. He also dealt in art. In his treatise on the rules of painting he argued that a painting should be a mirror of nature.

Yrjö Ollila's parents emigrated to America after his older brothers died, and a decorative painter became his guardian. He studied at the drawing school of the Finnish Art Society. Later he went to Paris on a state scholarship. In 1912 he joined the Septem group, whose members included Willy Finch and Magnus Enckell. They were Impressionists who pushed for pure colors. In 1919 he and the actress Elli Tompuri tried to start a theater for newer playwrights, but it went bankrupt a year later and he moved his family to France for seven years.

Eric Gill was born in Brighton and grew up in Chichester. In London he was an apprentice at a firm of ecclesiastical architects and took evening classes in stone masonry and calligraphy. Then he dropped architecture and set up a business cutting memorial inscriptions for buildings and headstones. He became a sculptor, letter cutter, typeface designer and printmaker. The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography calls him the greatest artist-craftsman of the twentieth century. His reputation changed after revelations that he sexually abused two of his daughters.

Paul Delaroche made his name with scenes from English and French history. He aimed for pragmatic realism and didn't glorify the people he painted. Marie-Antoinette, figures of Christianity and Napoleon Bonaparte all got the same treatment. He was a leading pupil of Antoine-Jean Gros, and later he taught Thomas Couture and Jean-Léon Gérôme, among others. His pictures are emotional like Romantic work. Yet they stay as detailed as Academic ones.

David Teniers the Younger learned to paint from his father, who made altarpieces and was often in financial trouble. The father's debts sometimes landed him in jail, so David had to copy old masters to support the family. Later he became court painter and curator of the collection of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, the Governor General of the Habsburg Netherlands. He made a printed catalogue of the Archduke's pictures. He also founded the Antwerp Academy, hoping to revive Flemish art after the deaths of Rubens and Van Dyck. He is now remembered as the leading Flemish genre painter of his day, known for peasants, tavern scenes and alchemists.

Tang Yin was a Ming dynasty painter who also wrote poems. Although he lived in the Ming period, many of his paintings, especially figures, borrowed elements from art that ran from before the Tang to the Song. He is counted among the Four Masters of the Ming dynasty, along with Shen Zhou and Qiu Ying. His influence on contemporaries such as Cai Han is notable. He was a talented poet too, and with Wen Zhengming and Zhu Yunming he was one of the Four Literary Masters of the Wuzhong Region.

Christian Griepenkerl is best known today as the professor who turned down Adolf Hitler's application to the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna. He was born to one of Oldenburg's leading families. On the advice of the landscapist Ernst Willers, he went to Vienna in late 1855 to join the private school for monumental painting that Carl Rahl had founded four years earlier. Rahl let several students help draft and carry out his paintings. Griepenkerl's first painting, Œdipus, Led by Antigone, won Rahl's approval.

Charles Willson Peale moved from his native Maryland to Philadelphia in 1775, inspired by the American Revolution. He set up a painting studio and joined the Sons of Liberty. During the war he served in the Pennsylvania Militia and the Continental Army, and he also sat in the Pennsylvania State Assembly. His portraits of leading American figures of the late 18th century are some of the most recognizable of that era. He was a scientist and naturalist too. In 1784 he founded the Philadelphia Museum, one of the first American museums.

Maurice Utrillo was born Maurice Valadon in Montmartre, and he is one of the few famous painters of Montmartre to have been born there. His mother, Suzanne Valadon, was an eighteen-year-old artist's model at the time. She never revealed who the father was. People have guessed at an amateur painter named Boissy, at Puvis de Chavannes, and even at Renoir. Utrillo specialized in cityscapes and belonged to the School of Paris.

Jacopo Bassano was born Jacopo dal Ponte and took the small town of Bassano del Grappa as his surname. He trained in his father's workshop and spent much of the 1530s painting in Venice. After 1539 he went back to Bassano and stayed there, continuing the family workshop. Eventually it included four of his sons. He often treated biblical subjects like scenes of country life, with peasants, animals and farmland painted in close detail. His pictures became popular in Venice and then across Europe.

Max Kurzweil moved near Vienna as a boy and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts there under Christian Griepenkerl and Leopold Carl Müller. He then went to the Académie Julian in Paris, where he exhibited his first painting at the Salon. He co-founded the Vienna Secession in 1897. He also edited and illustrated its influential magazine Ver Sacrum. Kurzweil taught at the Frauenkunstschule, an academy for women artists in Vienna. He won the Villa Romana prize in 1905, and his later work shows the influence of Edvard Munch and Ferdinand Hodler.

Kate Greenaway started out designing for the new greetings card market, producing Christmas and Valentine's cards. She had studied at four art schools, including the Slade. In 1879 the engraver and printer Edmund Evans printed her book Under the Window, and it was an instant best-seller. They kept working together through the 1880s and 1890s. Her children wear imaginary 18th-century costumes in a Queen Anne style. These pictures were extremely popular.

Félix Vallotton was a Swiss and French painter who helped develop the modern woodcut. His earliest paintings were influenced by Holbein and Ingres. In the 1890s he moved to a simpler style while he was with Les Nabis, and his woodcuts brought him international recognition. They use broad masses of black and white with minimal detail. Among them is a series of ten interiors called Intimités, which show charged domestic encounters. He painted portraits, landscapes, nudes and still lifes in an unemotional, realistic style.

Mauro Antonio Tesi is sometimes called Il Maurino, a name given to him by his patron Francesco Algarotti. He was largely self-taught. He worked as a decorative and architectural painter in churches and other buildings in Bologna and Florence. In 1764 he finished the nave ceiling frescoes for the small church of San Leone in Pistoia. He travelled with Algarotti and illustrated his writings. He also designed the funeral monument on the Campo Santo in Pisa. He is considered an early supporter of the Neo-classical style.

Halfdan Egedius was born in Drammen and grew up in Christiania, which is now Oslo. He began to paint and illustrate at five. By nine he was at the art school of Knud Bergslien. Later he studied with Erik Werenskiold, at the Harriet Backer art school, and in spring 1896 with Kristian Zahrtmann in Copenhagen. From the age of 15 he painted the landscape of Telemark. He died at 21.

Eadweard Muybridge was born Edward James Muggeridge in Kingston upon Thames. He changed his first name to Eadweard, which he took to be the original Anglo-Saxon form, and his surname to Muybridge, which he believed was just as archaic. In the 19th century American West he photographed Yosemite, San Francisco, the newly acquired Alaskan Territory, subjects of the Modoc War and lighthouses on the West Coast. He made his early moving picture studies in California. He is known for pioneering photographic studies of motion.

Lars Hertervig was born on the west coast of Norway, north of Stavanger, to a poor family of Quaker farmers. He studied painting at the Arts Academy of Düsseldorf from 1852 as the private pupil of Hans Gude. His semi-fantastical pictures drew on the coastal landscape of Ryfylke. Many of them are regarded as among the peaks of Norwegian painting.

Franz von Stuck showed a gift for drawing and caricature from an early age. He was born at Tettenweis near Passau, and at 15 he moved to Munich, where he stayed for life. He was best known for paintings of ancient mythology. The Sin won him substantial critical acclaim in 1892. He was also a sculptor, a printmaker and an architect. After he received the Order of Merit of the Bavarian Crown in 1906, which came with a title, people called him Ritter von Stuck.

Harald Sohlberg studied at the Royal School of Art and Design in Christiania and later trained under the graphic artist Johan Nordhagen. He went to Kristian Zahrtmann's art school too. He was also a pupil of Erik Werenskiold, Eilif Peterssen and Harriet Backer. He painted in the Neo-romantic style and is particularly known for his pictures of the Rondane mountains and the town of Røros. His most widely recognized painting, in several variations, is Winter's Night in Rondane.

Henriëtte Ronner-Knip was born in Amsterdam into a family of artists. Her father, Joseph August Knip, gave her first lessons. He also taught his youngest sister Henriëtte Geertruida Knip, who was her aunt. Her grandfather Nicolaas was an artist as well. She became a Dutch-Belgian painter, chiefly in the Romantic style, and she is best known for her animal paintings, especially of cats.

Nobody knows exactly when Titian was born. As an old man he told Philip II of Spain in a letter that it was 1474, but that seems most unlikely. Most modern scholars think the late 1480s is likelier. His father Gregorio was a soldier who worked mainly as a timber merchant and managed mines in the Cadore mountains. Titian's patrons ran from Venice to the north Italian princes, and finally the Habsburgs and the papacy. In 1590 Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo called him "the sun amidst small stars".

Albrecht De Vriendt came from a family of painters. His father was a decorative painter, and his brother Juliaan and sister Clementine became painters too. As a child he helped his father with decorative jobs. In 1865 he moved to Antwerp, where he studied under Victor Lagye and came under the influence of the history painter Jan August Hendrik Leys. Later he settled in Brussels and had five children. With Juliaan he travelled to Germany, Egypt and Palestine. The Egypt and Palestine trip produced many studies and a joint panorama called The Death of Christ. He also directed the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Antwerp.

Pierre Bonnard studied law to satisfy his father, a senior official in the French Ministry of War, and he began practicing as a lawyer. At the same time he took art classes at the Académie Julian, where he met Paul Sérusier and Maurice Denis. He sold his first commercial work in 1888, a poster design for France-Champagne. That helped him convince his family that he could make a living as an artist. From 1893 until her death he lived with Marthe de Méligny, who modeled for many of his paintings, and they married in 1925. He was a founding member of Les Nabis.

Carl Larsson grew up very poor in Stockholm. His father drank and raged, and his mother worked long hours as a laundress. At 13 a teacher at the school for poor children urged him to apply to the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts, and he was admitted. He felt shy and socially inferior at first, then gained confidence and became a central figure in student life. He moved to Paris in 1877 and spent several frustrating years there without success. Later he became known for his watercolors of idyllic family life. He considered Midwinter Sacrifice his finest work.

Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun sketched a bearded man at seven or eight, and her father, a portraitist, was so pleased that he started giving her lessons. He died when she was 12. She went on to become the portrait painter to Marie Antoinette. Over her career she created 660 portraits and 200 landscapes, and she was elected to art academies in ten cities. Joshua Reynolds was among those who rated her one of the greatest portraitists of her time. In her eighties she published her memoirs, which include advice for young portraitists.

Michelangelo was born in the small Tuscan town of Caprese. His family had been small-scale bankers in Florence for generations, but the bank failed. The Pietà and David were both sculpted before he turned 30. He didn't consider himself a painter, yet he made two of the most influential frescoes in Western art, on the ceiling and altar wall of the Sistine Chapel. At 71 he took over as architect of St. Peter's Basilica. He was the first Western artist whose biography was published in his lifetime. His contemporaries admired his terribilità, his ability to fill viewers with awe.

Ivan Aivazovsky was baptized Hovhannes, the son of an Armenian merchant in Feodosia in Crimea. At the Imperial Academy of Arts he was known as Gaivazovsky, and he became Aivazovsky while in Italy. He once signed a letter Giovani Aivazovsky. In a career of almost 60 years he created around 6,000 paintings, which made him one of the most prolific artists of his time. Most are seascapes, but he also painted battle scenes, Armenian themes and portraits. Anton Chekhov popularized the saying worthy of Aivazovsky's brush.

Ralph Earl taught himself to paint and spent many years as an itinerant painter. His father was a colonel in the Revolutionary army, but Earl was a Loyalist. In 1775 he visited the battle sites at Lexington and Concord, and with the engraver Amos Doolittle he drew four battle scenes that became pro-Revolutionary prints. Three years later he left his wife and daughter and escaped to England, disguised as the servant of a British army captain. In London he joined the studio of Benjamin West. Back in America he was jailed for debt and kept drawing portraits of his visitors while he was inside.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini was the sixth of thirteen children, born in Naples to the Mannerist sculptor Pietro Bernini. He was recognized as a prodigy at eight. Pope Paul V is said to have remarked that this child would be the Michelangelo of his age. Bernini became the leading sculptor of his time, and he is credited with creating the Baroque style of sculpture. He also designed fountains, churches and public squares. In the theatre he wrote and acted in plays, mostly Carnival satires, and he designed the stage sets and machinery for them.

David Roberts started out as a house painter and decorator in Scotland. In 1815 he went to Perth as foreman for the redecoration of Scone Palace. The next year he got a job painting scenery for a circus. That launched his career as a painter and designer of stage scenery. He toured England with the circus, and he was sometimes called on to take minor stage roles as a foil for the clowns. Then the Pantheon Theatre in Edinburgh failed. He went back to house painting.

Ambrosius Francken I was born in Herentals, the son of a painter, and his brothers Frans and Hieronymus became painters too. He worked as a journeyman in the busy Antwerp workshop of Frans Floris. Then he left for France, where Hieronymus was already working at Fontainebleau. No records remain of what Ambrosius did there. Around 1573 he was back in Antwerp and joined the Guild of Saint Luke. In 1577 he married a widow who was 30 years older than he was and had inherited a stone trading business. They kept it running, and it was very lucrative.

Clara Peeters is the best-known female Flemish artist of her era, and one of the few women working professionally in 17th-century Europe. Details of her life are unclear. A Clara Peeters was baptized in Antwerp in 1594, but that would make her 12 or 13 when she signed her first known painting in 1607. Some scholars doubt that, and think she was born in the 1580s. She specialized in still lifes with food, such as breakfast pieces and banquet pieces. In one painting she put her own reflection on the rim of a jug lid. Nobody has found a record of her death.

Marianne von Werefkin was born in Tula, the daughter of a Russian general who ended his career as commander of the Peter and Paul Fortress in Saint Petersburg. Her talent for drawing was discovered in 1874, and she soon had academic lessons. As a teenager she had a large studio in the fortress. She regarded her family's summer estate in Lithuania as her real home. In 1880 she became a private student of Ilya Repin. Before 1890 she made a name in realistic painting as the Russian Rembrandt of the Tsarist Empire. Later she worked in Germany and Switzerland and is known for Expressionist works.

Henry Keller led a generation of Ohio watercolor painters known as the Cleveland School. He studied in Cleveland and Munich. Later he taught at the Cleveland School of Art and ran a summer school in Berlin Heights, Ohio. His students included Charles Burchfield and Frank Wilcox. He specialized in animal life and watercolor. A cousin wrote that, as far as the cousin knew, he was the only noted artist who didn't smoke. In 1939 he was elected an Associate of the National Academy of Design.

Alexander Gardner was a Scot who wanted to build a cooperative community in the United States based on socialist values. In 1850 he and others bought land near Monona, Iowa, but he never lived there. Instead he went back to Scotland, where he became owner and editor of the Glasgow Sentinel. At the Great Exhibition in London he saw the photographs of the American Mathew Brady, and that started his interest in photography. He emigrated, became Brady's assistant, and was soon put in charge of Brady's Washington gallery. Allan Pinkerton later recommended him as chief photographer for the U.S. Topographical Engineers.

Frederic Remington was born in Canton, New York, in 1861. His father was a Union army colonel who later worked as a newspaper editor and postmaster. Remington was an only child and large for his age. He loved to hunt and ride. He was a poor student, particularly in math, which didn't bode well for his father's hope that he would attend West Point. From an early age he drew soldiers and cowboys. As an adult he specialized in Western American Art, with cowboys, Native Americans and the US Cavalry.
